## Solution

Let $N = 10^{2002}+1$. We seek the first three digits after the decimal point of $N^{10/7}$.

**Step 1: Factor out the power of 10.**

$$N = 10^{2002}\!\left(1+10^{-2002}\right), \qquad N^{10/7}=10^{2002\cdot 10/7}\!\left(1+10^{-2002}\right)^{10/7}.$$

Compute $2002\cdot 10 = 20020 = 7\times 2860$, so $2002\cdot\tfrac{10}{7}=2860$ exactly. Thus

$$N^{10/7}=10^{2860}\left(1+10^{-2002}\right)^{10/7}.$$

**Step 2: Binomial expansion.**

$$\left(1+10^{-2002}\right)^{10/7}=1+\tfrac{10}{7}\,10^{-2002}+\binom{10/7}{2}10^{-4004}+\cdots$$

All terms from the second-order term onward are $O(10^{-4004})$, so after multiplying by $10^{2860}$ they contribute $O(10^{-1144})$ — utterly negligible at the first three decimal places. Hence

$$N^{10/7}=10^{2860}+\tfrac{10}{7}\,10^{858}+O(10^{-1144}).$$

**Step 3: Extract the fractional part.**

Since $10^{2860}$ is an integer, the fractional part of $N^{10/7}$ equals the fractional part of $\tfrac{10}{7}\cdot 10^{858}=\tfrac{10^{859}}{7}$, up to a negligible $O(10^{-1144})$ correction.

Compute $10^{859}\bmod 7$. Since $10^6\equiv 1\pmod 7$ (as $142857\times 7=999999$) and $859=6\times 143+1$,

$$10^{859}\equiv 10^{1}\equiv 3\pmod 7.$$

Therefore $10^{859}=7q+3$ for some integer $q$, and

$$\frac{10^{859}}{7}=q+\frac{3}{7}=q+0.\overline{428571}\ldots$$

**Step 4: Read off the digits.**

The fractional part is $0.428571428571\ldots$, so the first three digits to the right of the decimal point are

$$\boxed{428}.$$
